items.title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
items.summary: The crash, between a moving train and another that was stopped further up the track, was caused by an "inexplicable" error, the transport minister said.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: 'Chaotic scenes' at site of Spain's deadly train crash
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Image caption, The force of the crash saw several carriage fall down an embankment
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Image caption, Some passengers said the piece of train track that speared through a carriage may have slowed the train down
Spanish journalist Antonio JimÃ©nez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old SebastiÃ¡n Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Most political parties in Spain cancelled their campaign events scheduled for Wednesday.
The exception was the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near CÃ³rdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.

items.title: Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
items.summary: Survivors of the train crash in Spain have spoken of their shock, panic and anger at the accident in Toledo province on Wednesday.
items.content:
Figure caption, Survivor describes being onboard when trains collided
It was approaching 08:30 (07:30 GMT) on a normal Wednesday. Two high-speed trains were travelling south from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville.
One, run by state-owned operator Renfe had 397 passengers on board. Ahead of it on the same line was a train of Iryo private operator with 147 passengers. A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
Then the impossible happened, Spain's transport minister said, as the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error".
It crashed into the back of the other train between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, about 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid.
Figure caption, Watch: "People flew off their seats," says passenger
Some of the passengers were asleep, some had already started their working day on laptops - and others scrolled through their apps on their phones.
The journey was interrupted with an announcement that there was congestion on the tracks. This lasted a few minutes - for some, a bit longer for others.
Tangui Binier, 22, was in the Iryo train, the front carriage, number eight. His father was in number seven.
Their train was one of six to have been ordered to stop at 08:30. A few minutes later, "the train started speeding", Binier told the BBC, "then it came to a sudden halt".
Baffled, he looked out of the window and saw "wires on the left side come down, and then there being just a lot of smoke behind us."
Spanish journalist Roberto GÃ³mez was dozing on the high-speed Renfe train which had stopped more than 25km (16 miles) away from Binier's.
It was a brief stop. A few minutes later, the train began to move again, he explained, and then the crash happened.
He did not know that at 08:36 his train had been ordered to proceed with the journey and some 17 minutes later the "truly unbelievable" happened, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.
"The impact was terrible," GÃ³mez told Onda Cero radio. "You can imagine, the carriage is completely destroyed. All the suitcases are all over the wrecked carriage."
GÃ³mez suffered only minor injuries but described another passenger falling on top of him and sustaining a deep gash on his head.
"We were able to help people who had suffered severe blows to their chest and ribs," he said.
Rafael Barcelo was in one of the worst-affected carriages. A bruise on his forehead makes him one of the lucky survivors. He was having a coffee at the time of the crash and "felt a huge impact".
"We were all thrown into the air," he told Reuters news agency at the site of the crash.
"I was travelling in coach seven, which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed. I at least counted eight victims in that coach," he said, visibly shocked.
Image caption, Rafael Barcelo: "I counted eight victims in that coach"
Even in the carriages farthest away from the impact on the Renfe train "everything was completely destroyed - the seats were detached, and most of the people who were travelling facing the same direction as the train were thrown into the air", according to Salvador Arriza.
"It was something brutal," he said, describing how some people "were trapped between the seats".
"What caught my attention is that in one of the coaches there was a piece of train track that went through the roof of the coach, and I think that might have helped to stop or reduce the inertia of the train."
Image caption, Salvador Arriza says a long piece of track that speared through the carriage roof may have slowed the train down
Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
SebastiÃ¡n Herrero was travelling in the train which was hit from the rear and the "terrible, terrible impact" threw him on to the seats in front.
"After we fell, there were many people with broken noses, broken arms... We started seeing smoke everywhere."
Image caption, The crash near Urda is Spain's worst rail disaster since 2013
Once the initial impact was over, passengers in Binier's carriage debated whether it was safe to leave because of the electrical wires strewn outside the train.
Some were worried about the risk of another train colliding and decided to exit.
"We did not know what had happened until we took a step outside, and there there was evidence of what had happened.
"We saw the other train behind ours and we saw our train completely flipped over and the back side full of debris," he told the BBC.
"When I got out of the train I was in complete shock, complete awe. There were people in danger, it was very hard to see, there was dead bodies, there was missing limbs. "
"I don't know if that is something I will ever recover from."
But the adrenaline kicked in, he said, and those like him who had not suffered any injuries went to help.
Among them was his dad, who he explained was "able to carry a girl to safety, with a broken hip".
It was not long before local people arrived, followed by the police and ambulance services of the Guardia Civil.
"I'm really one of the most fortunate people and the luckiest person. I feel like just I'm so fortunate and I see other people who are not so fortunate, and I see them very close up. Sometimes you just ask yourself 'Why me?'," he said.
Spain was already reeling from the Adamuz high-speed rail disaster outside CÃ³rdoba in January, in which 46 people died.
It happened on the same high-speed rail line, but much further south. So Wednesday's accident has raised many questions for the authorities.
"It isn't possible that our train was stopped for five or 10 minutes and that the other train wasn't told to stop," one of them said.
"How can this happen with the technology we have?," they added. "It's not normal. We weren't told anything. The person who should have been told something was the driver of the other train. We wouldn't have cared as long as the other train had been warned. I don't understand this."

items.title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
items.summary: More than 500 passengers were on board the trains when the crash occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Aerial footage shows train crash scene
Two trains have crashed in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.
Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.
So far at least 68 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.
The two trains crashed just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country barrelled into another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.
Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.
Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.
All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
Image source, 1vanta3 / X via Anadolu / Getty Images
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown.
Transport minister Oscar Puente has said a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre which decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
Audio recordings between train controllers in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another up ahead had stalled.

Image caption, Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, FÃ¡tima BÃ¡Ã±ez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition , and 15 more in a critical condition.
Image caption, A huge emergency response is underway
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de TransfusiÃ³n said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and AlcÃ¡zar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
The Spanish Civil Guard has set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and CÃ³rdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.
"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain , its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

items.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
items.summary: The week, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to 60,000 workers as it looks to curb costs.
items.content:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (Â£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.
On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).
Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.
Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.
The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.
Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres .
Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.
The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.

Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence
Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’
An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.
The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident , was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.
The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.
A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.
Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.
Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.
Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year, Panahi warned that the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.
“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”
‘I think of those I left behind in prison’: Iran’s Jafar Panahi on life as a banned film-maker
The latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.
The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated film The Seed of the Sacred Fig , told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”
Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.
She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.
The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”
In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.

The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.
Our central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks . As Heather Stewart and Jessica Elgot report, in his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn. That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London. Here is a summary of the main points in the budget, by Jasper Jolly and Peter Walker.
Here are comments on the budget from a Guardian panel, comprising Polly Toynbee, Hettie O’Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik, and John McDonnell.
Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds | Panel
Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.
Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Andy Burnham and John Healey discussing the budget this afternoon with people in the cafe of the Abbey community centre in Westminster. Photograph: Richard Pohle/Reuters Jim O’Neill , the former Goldman Sachs chief economist and a Treasury minister under David Cameron, told the PM programme that he thought it was sensible for John Healey not to “rock the boat” with this budget. He said his old City friends were pleasantly surprised by what was in it.
My friends in my old world of business and investing, from the ones that have contacted me, every single one of them has been slightly positively surprised by what was announced today.
Torsten Bell , the Treasury minister, has just finished an interview on Radio 4’s PM programme. Asked about claims (like this one , assuming the MP is being sarcastic, or ours at 8.50am ) that the budget did not live up to Andy Burnham’s ambitions to end 40 years of neoliberalism, Bell said he did not accept that. In many areas, the government was taking a very different approach, he argued. He said Margaret Thatcher hollowed out local government, while today’s fiscal devolution roadmap will reverse that. He also said the proposals to change the way energy pricing works (see 12.50pm ) would transformative.
Here is a chart from the fiscal devolution roadmap document setting out what rules will change, and when.
Fiscal devolution roadmap. Photograph: Treasury MSAs are mayoral strategic authorities, and FSA are foundation strategic authorities, equivalent bodies which do not have a mayor to lead them.
A Treasury minister has dismissed as “garbage” opposition claims that the small print in the budget book shows that John Healey is actually cutting defence spending.
The budget red book says that, while £42.6bn had been set aside for MoD spending in 2027-28, that has now been revised down to £41.1bn.
The Treasury says this is because less money than expected is needed for pensions. But James Cartlidge , the shadow defence secretary, said that not allocating the unused money for other areas of defence spending was “a complete dereliction of duty from the chancellor”.
And James MacClearly , the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, made the same argument. He said:
It is disgraceful that after pitching Labour as serious on defence, Healey and [Wes] Streeting are cutting the military’s resource budget by nearly £1bn next year. This will leave our troops worse off and undermine our security.
In response, Torsten Bell , a Treasury minister, posted this on social media.
Absolute garbage - this is a technical change that happens when public sector pension contributions change. There’s no impact on defence spending power & the Tories used the same mechanism in govt. What does matter for defence spending? The chancellor, who has increased it
Today’s ‘picky bits’ budget has pushed tough decisions into next year, says Tim Sarson, head of tax policy at KPMG UK:
“When it comes to tax rises, as expected with his options limited by the 2024 manifesto, the chancellor was left with a pick and mix or ‘picky bits’ approach.
Overall the announcements today will raise £7bn per year by 2031-32 with some winners and losers including a widely trailed bank surcharge, which came in lower than expected at 3% and further taxes on the gambling sector
James Smith, ING’s developed markets economist in the UK, says the budget has left more questions than answers.
How will the government account for higher inflation in departmental budgets? How will it fund defence? Both questions were left unanswered today. The government’s overall spending pot for government departments was left largely unchanged later this decade, despite a higher path for inflation and the chancellor’s reaffirmed commitment to 3% Nato spending by 2030. Implicitly, that pledge is being funded by squeezing other areas of government; the OBR’s numbers imply real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year for unprotected departments later this decade.
That almost certainly won’t happen – and this is before you take social care or any of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other bold policies into account.
These thorny issues have been punted into 2027, potentially in the autumn, when the government will have to unveil its long-awaited spending review.
The New Economics Foundation says the budget is a missed opportunity to bring down inflation, through more ambitious cost of living measures.
The chancellor has missed an opportunity to bring down inflation rates, according to analysis from the New Economics Foundation (NEF). The research suggests a more ambitious package of cost-of-living policies would take inflation from the OBR’s projected 3.64% to 2.88% by June 2027.
But Capital Economics say the chancellor has done enough to keep the markets on side.
Today’s UK budget announcement has proven the non-event that newly-minted Chancellor Healey had signalled in advance. While his first budget is hardly inspiring, it contrasts favourably with the initial efforts of some of his recent predecessors.
By sticking to a gradual fiscal tightening path, and to the expectations set over the past couple of months for a muddle-through budget, Healey has probably done enough to keep the Gilt market on side for now.
We think that Gilt yields will fall over the coming year as the UK’s fiscal risk premium remains contained and the Bank of England policy takes a less hawkish path than money markets discount.
The government needed to issue a ministerial direction to get UK Export Finance to approve a £3bn increase in lending for Ukraine, it emerged today. This is a procedure that happens when a civil servant judges that a decision is not justified under normal responsible public spending rules, and insists that it can only go ahead if a minister explicitly overrules the objections.
In his letter explaining the need for a ministerial direction, Tim Reid , UKEF’s chief executive, argued that this was not a core obligation for the agency (which is there to help British exporters, not to fight Russia) and that the risk of the £6.5bn not being paid back was too high.
UKEF has played a significant role in delivering the government’s support to Ukraine by staying on cover with £3.5bn of capacity to provide export finance, supporting strategically important transactions including the supply of nuclear fuel, reconstruction of critical infrastructure and air-defence missiles. These have supported Ukraine’s resilience at a critical time while also creating jobs and industrial capacity across the UK.
However, the financial risks associated with UKEF providing support in Ukraine remain far beyond those that we would normally be willing to accept. The probability of default and expected loss is exceptionally high …
UKEF is close to capacity against its existing £3.5bn limit. You have now asked me to consider a £3bn increase in UKEF’s cover limit, taking UKEF’s Ukraine country risk limit to £6.5bn.
In response , Jonathan Reynolds , the business secetary, said he was issuing a ministerial direction because “the United Kingdom has been steadfast in its support for Ukraine’s defence, economic resilience and long-term recovery, and I consider UKEF’s support to be an important component of that wider effort.”
Labour’s E mployment R ights A ct is likely to have a negative impact on the economy, the OBR says today.
This is the first time that the OBR has assessed the potential economic impacts of the ERA, which received royal assent at the end of last year.
And the fiscal watchdog has concluded the ERA will probably have a negative impact on potential output, though it isn’t making an explicit assessment today.
Our analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.
That fits with the government’s own analysis, which said the reforms could cost businesses up to £5bn a year.
Employment rights reforms ‘could cost UK businesses £5bn a year’
Earlier John Healey got an endorsement for what he said about defence spending from Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general. (See 2.15pm .)
George Robertson , the former Nato secretary general and the lead author of the strategic defence review, has also welcomed Healey’s defence announcements. (See 1.30pm .) He said:
John Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defence in his resignation letter, by setting a headmark for 3% in 2030.”
I am strongly in favour of innovative ways of financing defence – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defence. Today’s annoucements strengthens UK leadership in Nato once again.
In his speech Healey announced an extra £10bn in economic support for Ukraine. This Treasury news release explains where that money is going. It says:
The £10bn package includes £7bn of economic support being made available over three years, including up to £5.5bn of World Bank guarantees and a £500m grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility, mobilising £1.5bn of support for Ukraine.
Alongside this, there will be a £3bn increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) capacity for Ukraine, prioritised for military support. It will bring the total UKEF support to £6.5bn.
Traders on the floor of Saxo Bank today. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian Over at Saxo UK, traders report there was little drama in today’s budget.
“It was a boring budget” says Andrew Bresler , the chief executive of Saxo UK , adding:
They have been able to achieve what they set out to which is effectively no movement in financial markets.
Neil Wilson , an investor strategist at the bank, says the budget was “a nothing burger”, pointing out:
Business groups have given the budget a mixed reaction.
Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the CBI , welcomed some measures, but argued John Healey should have done more for growth. She said
On the face of it, this budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.
At a time of exceptional geopolitical pressures, using some fiscal headroom to absorb genuine short-term shocks is preferable to loading additional permanent costs onto business and weakening investment.
Slowing the convergence of youth rates with the national living wage is a sensible move in face of the Neets crisis and current labour market pressures. But the chancellor could have gone further. Reducing the cost of hiring by increasing the employer NICs threshold would have given firms more space to create entry-level jobs and boost employment.
Jonathan Geldart, director general at the Institute of Directors , said his members were relieved.
Business leaders will be relieved that the chancellor’s budget included no nasty surprises, having been conditioned in previous budgets to expect the worst. We very much welcome the numerous measures intended to support British start-ups and scale-ups, such as the new Founders’ Relief, Young Entrepreneurs Allowance and EMI2 [enterprise management incentive] share incentives (as well as support for small brewers).
What might at first blush be a case of small beer today could start adding up to something promising in the future.
But Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said the budget was a disappointment.
This budget should have been the moment to help small businesses with the soaring costs holding them back, and the taxes restricting job creation. Instead, they got nothing to ease sky-high energy bills and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable, while the increase in business rates relief excludes too many.
A JP Morgan spokesperson has criticised the decision to hike the UK’s bank tax today, arguing that targeting one of the UK’s most lucrative sectors “lacks principle”:
“We are committed to the country, and we recognise the cost of living challenges there and the global economic headwinds that it faces, but to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.
“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”
But despite the bank’s disappointment, JP Morgan is due to charge ahead with its £3bn new UK HQ, according to a source familiar with the matter.
JP Morgan to press on with London HQ despite new bank tax in ‘boring budget’ – business live
Kemi Badenoch’s reaction to the budget on behalf of the Conservative party was covered earlier, at 2.11pm . Here is some reaction from other oppostion parties.
The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey , told MPs that John Healey should have done more to address the problems with Brexit. He said:
I do think this budget will be more defined by Labour’s red lines on Europe and the Conservatives’ Brexit red tape, rather than faster growth.
And at the root of so much of what’s gone wrong in our country – the cost of living crisis, higher taxes, broken public services, empty high streets, the lack of jobs and opportunity – at the root of all of that is the lack of economic growth.
Our economy is being held back. British business is being held back, and it’s been held back above all by the terrible damage of the Conservative Brexit deal.
Ellie Chowns , the Green party Treasury spokesperson, said the budget was lacking in ambition.
You’d have thought that, after going to the trouble of ousting the last PM, taking his job, and installing a brand-new chancellor, Andy Burnham would be keen to ensure Labour displayed a bit more ambition at today’s budget than it did under his predecessor.
Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.
There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.
Nigel Farage , the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media , he said:
These are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.
The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.
By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …
We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.
Kirsty Blackman , the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:
The UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.
This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.
Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.
Ben Lake , Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.
Today’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.
After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition
The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.
Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.
Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts , Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), Rank Group (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year , also warned that closures and job losses would follow.
The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.
Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation ( including among economists and investors ) that he could seek to consolidate his position.
He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.
The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget .
“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.
“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.
“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”
He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.
“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”
Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.
Andrew Wishart , senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.
He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.
The big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.
More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”
Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management , says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.
Like last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.
“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”
Benjamin Jones , Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:
“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.
His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.
John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.
The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

items.title: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say - CBS News
items.summary: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say  CBS News<a href="https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihgFBVV95cUxQVzR0akhER3FqcmVpeEJQTFZqYVdhLVU3U2FiNWgtMDdYa0c3em11My1ORnlEdkxCY
items.content:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain , derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Aerial view of carriages and first responders on the site of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, Wednesday Oct. 28, 2026.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
One passenger said, "We were all thrown into the air." He said he was "reasonably OK" but that his friend was in much worse condition.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.
